offence_severity: Minimum: 6 months rigorous imprisonment, Maximum: 1 year rigorous imprisonment
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence indicated that the accused assaulted PW1's daughter-in-law to outrage her modesty, and the court accepted that the accused was not charged with an offence against her but was tried for it, leading to a failure of justice.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW1 and PW2, noting that their evidence showed the accused did not touch or abuse PW1, but touched PW1's daughter-in-law, leading to the conclusion that the accused was misled by the charge.
trial_duration: The accused was tried from 23.3.1996, the trial judgment was dated 2.2.2001, the High Court decision was on 16.3.2010, and the Supreme Court decision was on 7.9.2010.
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Vikas Sharma, K.M. Gupta, Praveen Swarup; Counsel for the State: Not stated.
investigation_status: FIR registered on 23.3.1996, charge sheet filed, trial completed.

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted under Sections 452 and 354 IPC, sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and a fine of Rs.1,000/-
appeal_history.high_court: Upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence from six to four months rigorous imprisonment
appeal_history.supreme_court: Allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction, and remitted the matter for a new trial

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused could be punished for assaulting and outraging the modesty of PW1's daughter-in-law, even though he was not charged with any offence with reference to PW1's daughter-in-law, on the ground that the error or omission in the charge did not prejudice the accused or result in failure of justice.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused was not required to defend himself against a charge that he assaulted and outraged the modesty of PW1's daughter-in-law, as the charge levelled against him was not proved, and thus he ought to have been acquitted.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the principles of fair play and natural justice embodied in Sections 211, 212, 215 and 464 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, emphasizing that an accused should know what is the charge against him to build his defence and that the main concern is whether the accused had a fair trial.
precedent_relied_upon: Willie (William) Staney v. State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 1956 SC 116; Gurbachan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1957 SC 623; Shamnsaheb M. Multtani vs. State of Karnataka 2001 (2) SCC 577; State of West Bengal vs. Laisal Haque AIR 1989 SC 129; State of A.P. vs. Thakkidiram Reddy 1998 (6) SCC 554; Dalbir Singh v. State of UP 2004 (5) SCC 334; Dumpala Chandra Reddy vs. Nimakayala Bali Reddy 2008 (8) SCC 339 and Sanichar Sahni vs. State of Bihar 2009 (7) sec 198
other_sentence_order: The matter is remitted to the trial court with a direction for a new trial after framing a charge by substituting the words 'her daughter-in-law Sheela Devi' for the words 'abovenamed Prakashi Devi', in the second part of the charge.
